strengths: First systematic study of adversarial robustness in deep speech denoising models, addressing an important security gap in widely-deployed high-stakes applications

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 DNS models with varying architectures, multiple environmental settings (SNRs, reverb), threat models (white-box, transfer, over-the-air), and metrics, with 20 random seeds for statistical rigor
Methodologically sound approach using principled psychoacoustic masking with thoughtful enhancements (temporal pre/post-masking, threshold adjustments) and proper formalization of threat models

Strong empirical findings showing all tested models vulnerable to imperceptible perturbations across diverse settings, including at 70 dB SNR (near zero-noise setting) and in simulated over-the-air scenarios
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations, including FSN+'s pseudo-robustness from exploding gradients, non-transferability of attacks, and lack of user study validation
Clear, well-organized presentation with good motivation and thorough related work discussion
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: directly applies established attack techniques from prior audio adversarial work (Schönherr et al. 2018, Qin et al. 2019) to new domain; perceptibility enhancements (12 dB threshold shift, pre/post-masking) are incremental

Practical threat model significantly more constrained than framing suggests: (1) targeted attacks largely ineffective—authors admit even high STOI outputs are perceived as 'faint robotic hints'; (2) attacks completely non-transferable between models; (3) requires white-box gradient access; (4) universal perturbations fail

Imperceptibility claims not validated: no ABX or user studies provided; for over-the-air attacks, authors loosen perceptibility constraint (12→6 dB) and acknowledge 'slight crackling to sometimes be audible', contradicting imperceptibility claims

Loss function breakdown: STOI fails as maximization objective for targeted attacks; DNN-based metrics perform poorly; PESQ unavailable due to licensing; suggests optimization may not align with perceptual attack success
Shallow defense analysis: only evaluates Gaussian noise defense; no adversarial training or other standard defenses; provides minimal practical guidance for practitioners

Limited mechanistic understanding of vulnerability: no analysis of why DNS models are more vulnerable than image denoising models; Table 1 shows robustness uncorrelated with architecture but analysis ends there; FSN+'s exploding gradient pseudo-defense not deeply analyzed

Experimental design concerns: varying iteration counts across models (20K→5K) to fit 1-hour budget; over-the-air optimization uses multiple heuristics without sensitivity analysis; perturbation selection based on loss rather than perceptual validation
Dataset limitations: English read speech only; 5-second clips; single-channel; limited evidence of generalization to diverse real-world speech
Reproducibility gaps: no code released; some implementation details unclear; varying iteration counts complicate replication

strengths: Addresses important security vulnerability in widely-deployed DNS models used in safety-critical applications (hearing aids, emergency communications, air-traffic control)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning 4 DNS models, multiple SNR/reverb conditions, simulated over-the-air attacks, and 5 distinct metrics with thorough ablations
Human study validation with transcription and ABX tasks conducted by audio professionals, providing credibility beyond computational metrics alone
Principled auditory masking methodology with temporal pre/post-masking and RIR-aware optimization is technically sound and well-motivated
Honest reporting of negative results (UAPs ineffective, transfer failures, targeted attacks subjectively unsuccessful) strengthens credibility and provides important practical insights
Excellent presentation, detailed appendices, and commitment to reproducibility (code and samples promised to be released)
Thoughtful practical threat analysis acknowledging attacker assumptions and limitations of the threat model
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core technique is standard PGD with auditory masking thresholds from prior ASR work; temporal masking and offsets are incremental enhancements rather than novel contributions

Marginal evidence for imperceptibility claim: ABX study shows only 59% accuracy vs 50% baseline with 95% lower CI of 0.478 (below chance); substantial participant/sample variance; statistical significance not established

Practical threat more limited than framed: white-box access required, transfer attacks fail (black-box infeasible), attacks are offline/per-utterance not streaming, targeted attacks don't subjectively work despite objective metrics

Shallow defense evaluation: only Gaussian noise baseline tested; established defenses (adversarial training, randomized smoothing) not evaluated; acknowledges adaptive attacks would likely bypass but doesn't explore; no constructive solutions provided

Over-the-air realism concerns: simulation only (no physical experiments), assumes linear acoustic propagation, real playback chains introduce uncharacterized nonlinearities/compression, 6 dB masking relaxation for OTA indicates practical difficulty
FSN+ robustness primarily from exploding gradients (not architecture), acknowledged as trivially bypassable via known techniques, weakening claims about understanding model robustness factors

Human study limitations: small sample (15 from single lab), ABX results not statistically significant, unclear if findings generalize to general population, 5-second clips (vs 10-second) for practical reasons
Optimization objective limitations: STOI breaks down for targeted attacks (high STOI ≠ intelligibility), PESQ unavailable, DNN-based metrics ineffective, limiting targeted attack feasibility
Limited model scope: only 4 DNS models, no token-based models (acknowledged), MP-SENet truncated to 5 seconds due to memory constraints, broader landscape unexplored

strengths: Addresses an important but understudied vulnerability in safety-critical DNS systems (hearing aids, emergency communications, ATC)
Comprehensive experimental coverage: 4 models, diverse SNR/reverb settings, over-the-air simulation with real RIRs, multiple metrics
Psychoacoustically principled attack methodology with rigorous masking enhancements (temporal pre/post-masking, threshold offsets)
Human validation with transcription and ABX studies demonstrating unintelligibility and marginal imperceptibility
Excellent reproducibility: multiple seeds (20), detailed hyperparameters, promised code/samples, honest reporting of negative results
Valuable mechanistic insight: FSN+ robustness comes from gradient instability (pseudo-robustness) rather than architecture
Results generalize across diverse conditions (70 dB near-clean to -10 dB noisy, with/without reverb)
Methodologically rigorous: proper statistical tests (two-way bootstrap with crossed effects), ablations validating design choices
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: core approach (PGD + psychoacoustic masking) closely follows Qin et al. [38] and Schönherr et al. [45]; main contributions are domain adaptation and STOI as loss, which are engineering-level rather than algorithmic innovations

Practical threat model is significantly constrained: attacks require white-box access; naive transfer fails across architectures; weak cross-checkpoint transfer even within same model family; pure black-box attacks not thoroughly explored

Human study limitations substantially weaken imperceptibility claims: small sample (n=15 from single lab), ABX results statistically marginal (59% mean with 95% CI lower bound 0.478, not significantly above 50% chance), only 3/4 models evaluated, 5-second clips shorter than typical conversations

Targeted attacks are largely unsuccessful: STOI metric breaks down as maximization objective; subjective evaluation reveals targets barely audible even at high STOI; cross-speaker and synthesized targets ineffective
Over-the-air attacks only simulated: real playback chains introduce nonlinearities, gain control, codec compression not modeled; no actual over-the-air validation experiments

Defense analysis is superficial: only Gaussian noise baseline evaluated; no adversarial training or principled defenses; Gaussian noise already moderately effective, limiting impact of security findings

Limited mechanistic understanding: paper documents vulnerability but provides minimal insight into why DNS models fail to reject adversarial noise; no analysis of what architectural properties or training procedures would improve robustness
Metric-specific results: attack success varies across metrics (Figure 11); STOI chosen partly due to PESQ licensing issue; unclear which metric best captures intelligibility
